name: World Vision US: domestic programmes (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: donated goods passed to US churches, schools and nonprofits.
summary: World Vision US's domestic programmes ($231 million in fiscal 2025) pass donated corporate goods (clothing, household goods, school and building supplies: $206 million at wholesale value) to US churches, schools and nonprofits from its warehouses. Valued on the site's one log-income scale at low-income Americans' consumption, at 60% of their recorded value as goods given in kind, a dollar does far less than a dollar abroad: low because the goods go to people in a rich country, where they add little to consumption, not because the work is badly run. World Vision US publishes no count of the households its goods reach, so reach is the goods' value over a judged amount per household and the model is discounted for missing data; the biggest uncertainties are what the goods are worth to families and how many would have reached them anyway.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: World Vision US, domestic programmes

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Domestic programmes, fiscal 2025, without the donated goods
rows.explainer: World Vision US's domestic line (Form 990) less the donated goods it handed out: the warehouses, freight, partner support and staff. The goods enter the credit share below (Convention 2).

rows.label: Total expenses without donated goods, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: World Vision US's total expenses less all donated goods and food commodities it passed on, at home and abroad.

rows.label: Programme expenses without donated goods, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: Programme expenses less the same donated goods and commodities.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: World Vision US's management and fundraising spread over its programmes by cost, as in its international model.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled program, including overhead
rows.explainer: The domestic line's own spending plus its share of overhead.

rows.label: Donated goods handed out in the US, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: Household goods, clothing, toys, building supplies, hygiene and school supplies at wholesale value (KPMG note 16: domestic gifts-in-kind used, $206.0M).

rows.label: Goods value per household reached in a year (wholesale)
rows.explainer: World Vision US publishes no count of the US households its goods reach. Partners hand out a few bags of clothing, hygiene kits, school supplies or household goods per family; building supplies for home repairs and disaster recovery go to fewer households at higher value. Judgment $180 a household a year ($60-500).

rows.label: Households reached in the year
rows.explainer: Goods handed out over the value per household: about 1.1 million households at the best guesses.

rows.label: People per household
rows.explainer: The site's US household size: families with children are the main recipients (school supplies, clothing), larger than the poorest fifth's average of 1.6.

rows.label: People reached
rows.explainer: People reached.

rows.label: Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context.

rows.label: Life-satisfaction gain per person-year
rows.explainer: 0: the goods' value is counted below as income; counting their relief as wellbeing too would count it twice.

rows.label: Years the wellbeing effect lasts
rows.explainer: Not used (no wellbeing effect counted).

rows.label: WELLBYs per person
rows.explainer: Point-years, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: What the goods are worth to the family, as a share of their recorded value
rows.explainer: Two steps: the donors' wholesale value of surplus stock against what it would sell for (@united_states.donated_goods_value_vs_recorded, 0.85) and what goods given in kind are worth to a family against cash (@aid_value.inkind_goods_vs_cash, 0.7): about 0.6. Unused goods are in implementation_adj, not here.

rows.label: Value of the goods to each person, per year (US$)
rows.explainer: About {{row:value_per_person}} a person a year at the best guesses.

rows.label: US consumption per person (Consumer Expenditure Survey)
rows.explainer: The site's US survey consumption per person.

rows.label: Poorest fifth's consumption per person, as a share of the US average
rows.explainer: The site's per-person anchor: the poorest fifth's household spending over the average, per person (poorer households are smaller).

rows.label: Recipients' consumption per person against the poorest fifth's
rows.explainer: Families with children in Title I school districts and disaster-hit households are larger than the poorest fifth's average household (1.6 people), so their spending per person is lower; some recipients are better off. Judgment 0.67 (0.45-1.05).

rows.label: Recipients' consumption per person, as a share of the US average
rows.explainer: The anchor times the judged gap: about 0.45.

rows.label: Recipients' consumption per person per year
rows.explainer: Recipients' consumption per person per year.

rows.label: Years the gain counts
rows.explainer: 1: a year's goods.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.explainer: The site's one log-income scale at the recipients' own consumption.

rows.label: Health gained per person (DALYs)
rows.explainer: 0: no evidence that donated household goods, clothing or supplies change health in the US.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person
rows.explainer: 0: none expected from these goods.

rows.label: Share of deaths under five (not used)
rows.explainer: No deaths averted are counted.

rows.label: Share of deaths 5-14 (not used)
rows.explainer: No deaths averted are counted.

rows.label: Share of deaths 15-49 (not used)
rows.explainer: No deaths averted are counted.

rows.label: Value of a death averted
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by the age band of each death, times your value of a life: the site's one value of a death.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 1: the value is the goods at a judged share of their recorded value, which needs no effect study; the valuation doubt is in inkind_cash_equivalence and unused goods in implementation_adj. 0.9 at the low end for a recorded value that may not match what was handed out.

rows.label: Share of the goods that would have reached similar families through another charity
rows.explainer: Without World Vision, corporate surplus goes to other in-kind networks (Good360 and similar), sale to liquidators, or landfill. Good360 and World Vision compete for the same donors; judgment a quarter (10-45%) would have reached similar families anyway.

rows.label: Share that would have been sold off cheaply instead
rows.explainer: Liquidators and discount stores sell surplus at a fraction of wholesale, some of it to low-income buyers. Judgment 25% (10-40%); the rest is destroyed or landfilled.

rows.label: Share of the goods' value low-income buyers would have got from the sold-off goods
rows.explainer: Discounted goods give buyers some of the value (they pay most of it) and only some buyers are poor. Judgment 30% (10-50%).

rows.label: Share of the goods families wouldn't have got anyway
rows.explainer: What the families gain that the goods' other uses wouldn't have given similar families: about 67% at the best guesses.

rows.label: Donated goods handed out, at US market value
rows.explainer: The goods at the donors' wholesale value, times the shared ratio of market to recorded value.

rows.label: Partners' resources, as a share of World Vision's own and the goods
rows.explainer: Partner churches and schools add volunteer time and space to hand the goods out (World Vision US counts 28,224 volunteers across all its work, 990 Part I). 18% (5-43%).

rows.label: World Vision's share of the resources behind the goods reaching families
rows.explainer: Convention 2: World Vision's own spending over that plus the donated goods at market value, plus partners' resources.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Share of the goods that reach families and get used
rows.explainer: Some goods sit in partners' storage, go unused or are passed on. 85% (70-95%).

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: The goods are donated; cash pays for the logistics that bring them in, so a dollar's leverage is in the goods' value already. 1 (0.95-1.05).

rows.label: Missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: World Vision US publishes no count of the households its US goods reach; reach and value are judgments. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Unmodelled: school supplies' gain in attendance and teachers' time
rows.explainer: School and office supplies are about 1-1.5% of the domestic goods (KPMG note 16: $3.2M of school and office supplies received in all, against $206M of goods used at home); their learning and teachers' time saved beyond their value: +0.3% (0 to +1%).

rows.label: Unmodelled: goods arriving when a disaster leaves families short
rows.explainer: Goods after hurricanes and floods are worth more than their price while shops are shut: +1% (0 to +3%).

rows.label: Unmodelled: free goods displacing local shops' sales
rows.explainer: Free clothing and household goods take some sales from small local shops and thrift stores: -0.5% (-2% to 0).

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The signed items above. Home repairs' lasting value is not here: a durable good's price already covers its years of use.
